title: The Long Walk: the Thembu Boy, Prisoner 466/64, and the Terraces of the Union Buildings
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Mvezo, the birth on the Mbashe
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the umzi of the Madiba clan on the banks of the Mbashe river a son is born to Nonqaphi Nosekeni and Nkosi Mphakanyiswa Gadla Mandela, principal counsellor to the Thembu royal house. They name him Rolihlahla, which in Xhosa means pulling the branch of a tree, and which the village translates as troublemaker. His father holds a chieftainship by appointment of a colonial magistrate, and by the same authority can be stripped of it. The Thembu kingship the boy is born beside is a kingship the empire licenses.
suggested_refs: The Mandela homestead at Mvezo, Mbashe district, Eastern Cape
sources: South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
Nelson Mandela Foundation, biography

stops.name: Qunu, the herdboy and the English name
stops.date_confidence: conflicted: Long Walk to Freedom and the Nelson Mandela Foundation place the loss of the chieftainship and the move to Qunu within a year of the 1918 birth, with Mandela an infant; SAHO and Wikipedia give 1926, year only. The conflict is recorded, not resolved. A circulating '1 October 1926' is rejected: no reachable source supports day-level precision.
stops.campa: His father is stripped of the chieftainship in a quarrel with the local magistrate, and the family moves to Qunu, a valley of grass huts and grazing. Mandela herds sheep and calves, moulds oxen out of clay, fights with sticks, and is sent to the Wesleyan mission school, where a teacher gives him the English name Nelson because the school requires that every child have one. He calls these the happiest years of his childhood. Ninety-five years later he is buried on this ground, in a grave he chose himself.
suggested_refs: The village of Qunu, Eastern Cape, childhood home and burial ground
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
Nelson Mandela Foundation, biography
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

stops.name: Mqhekezweni, the Great Place of the regent
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the coordinates of the historic Great Place are approximate, conceded as such by the source note, and the entry is therefore [R] rather than [A]
stops.campa: His father dies and the nine-year-old is delivered to Chief Jongintaba Dalindyebo, acting regent of the Thembu, who takes him as a ward and raises him beside his own son Justice. At the Great Place he sits at the edge of the tribal council and watches men speak in turn until the last has finished, the regent speaking only at the end. The old men teach him the praise-names of the Thembu kings and the wars they were given for. He is being raised for the counsellorship his father held, in a court a magistrate can dissolve.
suggested_refs: The Great Place at Mqhekezweni, seat of the Thembu regency
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Tyhalarha, the circumcision lodge on the river
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the site is described in Long Walk to Freedom but is not GPS-fixed in the record
stops.campa: At sixteen he goes with a group of Thembu boys to a lodge on the banks of the Mbashe for the ulwaluko, the Xhosa initiation that makes a boy a man. The wound is dressed, the huts are burned, the initiates are painted white and then washed clean in the river. At the ceremony Chief Meligqili rises and tells the new men they are slaves in their own country, their manhood a promise nobody intends to keep, their fields and their labour already owned. Mandela is annoyed by the speech and carries it for thirty years.
suggested_refs: The Tyhalarha initiation site on the Mbashe river
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994), ch. 3

stops.name: Clarkebury, the Methodist institute
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The regent sends him to the largest Methodist institution for Africans in Thembuland to read for the Junior Certificate. He arrives in his guardian's cast-off trousers, cut down and held up with string, and is laughed at for his country manners. He works, and the laughter stops. The principal, Reverend Harris, is a great-grandson of King Ngubengcuka and runs the school on English lines and English hours, and Mandela watches him more closely than the syllabus.
suggested_refs: Clarkebury Boarding Institute, Engcobo
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

stops.name: Healdtown, the college at Fort Beaufort
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years; the geography lens gives the span as 1937-1939 and the coordinate as -32.755 / 26.65, both corrected here. SAHO dates matriculation to 1938, and the site sits nearer -32.73 / 26.72
stops.campa: Two years at the Wesleyan college favoured by Thembu royalty, drilled in English manners and Protestant time by a headmaster who tells the students he is descended from the duke who beat Napoleon. Mandela runs long distance and boxes. In his last year the Xhosa poet Krune Mqhayi comes to the hall in a leopard-skin kaross carrying an assegai and performs praise poetry for his own nation, and the boys, schooled for years in the empire's manners, get to their feet and shout for him.
suggested_refs: Healdtown Methodist College, Fort Beaufort
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

stops.name: Fort Hare, the seat refused
stops.date_confidence: attested; the chronology lens dates enrolment to 1940 and says expelled, both corrected. Enrolment 1939, suspension after the first year in 1940, and suspension rather than expulsion
stops.campa: At the only university open to black South Africans he rooms near Oliver Tambo, argues with Kaiser Matanzima, and is elected to the Student Representative Council in a boycott election most students refuse to vote in. He resigns the seat on the principle that it was won from an empty ballot. The principal orders him to take it up or leave. He leaves, and never finishes the degree. At the Great Place the regent hears him out, and then tells him a wife has been chosen.
suggested_refs: The University of Fort Hare, Alice, Eastern Cape
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
Wikipedia, 'Nelson Mandela'
University of Fort Hare records

stops.name: Crown Mines, the night watchman
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1941; the month is inferred
stops.campa: He runs from an arranged marriage the regent has made for him and reaches Johannesburg with Justice, the two of them lying about their errand. His cousin Piliso, an employment agent, places him as a night watchman at the Crown Mines compound: a boarded room, a whistle, a lamp, and a sign at the gate. The lie is discovered within weeks and he is put out. Lodging in George Goch township, he meets Walter Sisulu, an estate agent, who sends him to the firm of Lazar Sidelsky for his articles of clerkship.
suggested_refs: The Crown Mines compound and George Goch township, Johannesburg
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Alexandra, the room in the Xhoma yard
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1941-1946; the month is inferred
stops.campa: He rents a tin-roofed room in the Xhoma family's backyard in Alexandra, a township of open sewers, gangs, paraffin lamps, and no electricity, where Africans may legally own the ground beneath their houses. He walks six miles each way to save the bus fare and reads by candle. He calls it, without irony, his beloved home. Alexandra is one of the few places in the Transvaal where the land under a black man's feet is his own. The state spends the next forty years trying to remove the township and does not manage it.
suggested_refs: The Xhoma family yard, Alexandra township, Johannesburg
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Witwatersrand, the only African in the faculty
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1943-1949
stops.campa: He enrols for a law degree as the only black African student in his faculty, sits in lecture halls where some classmates will not take the seat beside him, and finds the others: Joe Slovo, Ruth First, Ismail Meer, the white and Indian radicals of Johannesburg. He eats in Meer's flat at Kholvad House when the curfew catches him out, and sleeps on the floor. He never finishes the degree. Twenty years later Slovo has written the guerrilla plan the police lift out of a coal shed at Rivonia.
suggested_refs: The University of the Witwatersrand law faculty, Johannesburg
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Orlando West, the house on Vilakazi Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1946 for the move; the day is defaulted
stops.campa: He and Evelyn Mase move into a municipal matchbox of two rooms in Orlando West: red polished cement floor, no ceiling, a bucket latrine, a candle. Thembekile is born, then Makaziwe, who dies at nine months, then Makgatho. In 1944 he has joined the African National Congress and helped found its Youth League with Sisulu and Tambo, impatient with the old men's petitions. In 1948 the National Party wins the election on the word apartheid, and the argument about petitions is settled by the other side.
suggested_refs: 8115 Vilakazi Street, Orlando West, Soweto, now the Mandela House Museum
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
Mandela House Museum, 8115 Vilakazi Street
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

stops.name: Marshall Square, the first cell
stops.date_confidence: corrected; the geography lens dates this detention to 22 June 1952 and ties it to a Durban rally. He addressed the Durban rally on 22 June but was arrested in Johannesburg on the night of 26 June, the campaign's launch date, for a curfew violation
stops.campa: The Defiance Campaign against unjust laws opens on the twenty-sixth of June: volunteers walk through the whites-only doors, sit on the whites-only benches, break the curfew, and go quietly when the police come. Mandela is volunteer-in-chief. On the first night he is taken in Johannesburg with Walter Sisulu and some fifty others and held in the central police cells. Eight and a half thousand are arrested before the year is out. In December he is convicted, sentenced, suspended, and banned.
suggested_refs: Marshall Square police cells, central Johannesburg
sources: Wikipedia, 'Defiance Campaign'
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

stops.name: Kliptown, the Freedom Charter read aloud
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Three thousand delegates gather on a dusty sports field at Kliptown and adopt, clause by clause, a document assembled from scraps of paper collected across the country: South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white. Each clause is read in three languages and answered with a shout of Afrika. Mandela, under a banning order, watches from the edge of the crowd in disguise. On the second day the police close the field, photograph every delegate, and take the papers away as evidence of treason.
stops.quote: We believe that South Africa belongs to all the people who live in it, and not to one group, be it black or white.
stops.quote_source: Nelson Mandela, Statement from the Dock, Rivonia Trial, Pretoria, 20 April 1964, United Nations archived text (spoken nine years later, restating the claim adopted at Kliptown)
suggested_refs: The Congress of the People site, Kliptown, Soweto
sources: South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: The Drill Hall, the wire cage
stops.date_confidence: corrected; the geography lens dates the Drill Hall opening to 5 December 1956, the date of the dawn arrests. The preliminary hearing opened on 19 December. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the canonical Johannesburg pin in mahatma_gandhi.journey.json
stops.campa: At dawn on the fifth of December the police take one hundred and forty people from their beds across the country; one hundred and fifty-six are charged with treason. On the nineteenth they are driven to the Drill Hall, where the state has built a wire cage in the middle of the floor to hold them. Fifty years before, on this same ground, Mohandas Gandhi swore three thousand Transvaal Indians to defy the registration law. The trial runs four years; in March 1961 the twenty-eight still standing are acquitted.
suggested_refs: The Drill Hall, Twist Street, Johannesburg, and the Empire Theatre site of the 1906 satyagraha oath
sources: Wikipedia, '1956 Treason Trial'
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
mahatma_gandhi.journey.json (canonical Johannesburg pin)

stops.name: Pretoria Local Prison, the state of emergency
stops.date_confidence: attested; the chronology lens dates the Sharpeville massacre to 21 March 1961, an error of one year, corrected here to 1960. No Sharpeville coordinate is carried by the verified pool, so the massacre is narrated here rather than given a pin of its own
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of March police at Sharpeville fire into a crowd protesting the pass laws and kill sixty-nine people, many of them shot in the back. The government declares a state of emergency, bans the ANC outright, and holds Mandela without charge for five months in Pretoria Local Prison. He comes out into a country where his organisation is a crime. The Sharpeville dead are buried together at Vereeniging and the pass laws stand unaltered. Within eighteen months he is drafting the founding statement of an army.
stops.quote: Fifty years of non-violence had brought the African people nothing but more and more repressive legislation, and fewer and fewer rights.
stops.quote_source: Nelson Mandela, Statement from the Dock, Rivonia Trial, Pretoria, 20 April 1964, United Nations archived text
suggested_refs: Pretoria Local Prison; the Sharpeville massacre site, Vereeniging
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sharpeville massacre'
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

stops.name: Liliesleaf Farm, the caretaker David Motsamayi
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1961-1962 for the residence; the month is inferred
stops.campa: In a whitewashed outbuilding on a smallholding at Rivonia a man in blue overalls answers to David Motsamayi and tells callers he is the caretaker. He is commander-in-chief of Umkhonto we Sizwe, the Spear of the Nation, founded that year to carry out sabotage against installations rather than against people. The newspapers call him the Black Pimpernel because the police cannot find him. He cooks, he reads, he drafts operational plans, and he stores the papers in the coal shed.
stops.quote: I was one of the persons who helped to form Umkhonto we Sizwe.
stops.quote_source: Nelson Mandela, Statement from the Dock, Rivonia Trial, Pretoria, 20 April 1964, United Nations archived text
suggested_refs: Liliesleaf Farm, Rivonia, Johannesburg
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
Liliesleaf Trust
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

stops.name: Addis Ababa, the conference of the free states
stops.date_confidence: attested; the chronology lens attaches this date to his departure from South Africa, which was 11 January 1962. The date belongs to the PAFMECSA address, three weeks later
stops.campa: He leaves South Africa on the eleventh of January without a passport and surfaces three weeks later in Addis Ababa, in khaki, addressing the Pan-African Freedom Movement conference as the delegate of a banned organisation. He asks the free states of Africa for money, for weapons, and for ground on which to train men. Thirteen months earlier Patrice Lumumba was killed in Katanga, and every delegate in the hall knows what independence has already cost. Selassie's officers agree to take his recruits.
suggested_refs: The PAFMECSA conference hall, Addis Ababa, February 1962
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
patrice_lumumba.journey.json

stops.name: Cairo, the republic that stayed
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the verified pool dates the Cairo visit to 1962 without a month
stops.campa: In Cairo he studies a state that threw the British out and kept them out. He takes notes on land reform and on how a poor country feeds itself while defying a rich one, and tours factories and cooperatives with the seriousness of a man expecting to govern. He spends a morning in the Egyptian Museum among four thousand years of African government. He is travelling on borrowed papers, with no army behind him and a sabotage campaign three months old at home.
suggested_refs: Nasser's Cairo, studied as a model of post-colonial administration
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Monrovia, the presidents of the new states
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the pool dates the West African leg to 1962 without months. Dakar and Lagos are attested stops on the same leg and are named here rather than given pins of their own
stops.campa: He crosses West Africa with a bag and a false name, asking heads of state for money: Tubman in Monrovia, who gives him five thousand dollars and a promise of training; Senghor's ministers in Dakar; the officials of the federation in Lagos. These states are three and four years old, their flags still new, and they receive a wanted man from a country that will not be free for another twenty-eight years as though he already represented a government, because in their reckoning he does.
suggested_refs: Monrovia, Dakar and Lagos, stations of the 1962 fundraising tour
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Accra, the flagship of the free continent
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the pool dates the Accra visit to 1962 without a month
stops.campa: In Nkrumah's Ghana, five years independent and the first of them all, Mandela sees the proposition tested in daylight: an African government running an African country, its mistakes as much its own as its revenues. He is received by officials of the Bureau of African Affairs, which funds liberation movements across the continent out of Accra, and he is asking men in Johannesburg to accept prison and death on the argument that this can be done. He will not see a self-governing black state at home for thirty-two more years.
suggested_refs: Nkrumah's Accra, first capital of independent sub-Saharan Africa
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Oujda, the camp on the Algerian border
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the geography lens places this training at Rabat, 34.0209 / -6.8416, corrected here to Oujda, the Algerian FLN's external-army base in eastern Morocco, approximately 34.68 / -1.91. The coordinate is approximate
stops.campa: At the base the Algerian Front de Liberation Nationale keeps on Moroccan soil near the border, Mandela is taught demolitions, mortars and the arithmetic of a guerrilla army by officers who have spent seven years fighting the French. Their lesson is political rather than military: the aim is not to beat the enemy's army but to destroy the belief that his order is permanent, and to keep the international ground moving under him. He watches an FLN parade and takes the salute.
suggested_refs: The FLN external-army base at Oujda, eastern Morocco
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: London, ten days in the imperial city
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1962; the day is inferred
stops.campa: He spends ten days in London, illegally and unphotographed, seeing Oliver Tambo, who runs the ANC's external mission from a flat in the north of the city, and meeting Labour and Liberal members of Parliament who will raise his name in the Commons. He walks past Westminster Abbey and the Houses of Parliament, the buildings of the government that wrote the laws of his childhood, and finds that he wants to look at them. Then he flies back into Africa, toward a roadblock in Natal.
suggested_refs: The ANC external mission office, London, 1962
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Howick, the roadblock on the Durban road
stops.date_confidence: attested; the roadside GPS is approximate per the source note
stops.campa: Seventeen months underground end on the Durban road outside Howick. He is driving back from briefing Chief Albert Luthuli, wearing a chauffeur's white coat, when a Ford full of police pulls level and waves the car down. He gives the name David Motsamayi; the officer recites his real one. Somebody has told them. The belief that the tip reached the security police through American or British intelligence is long-standing and has never been documented. He is sentenced to five years.
stops.quote: I am a convicted prisoner serving five years for leaving the country without a permit and for inciting people to go on strike at the end of May 1961.
stops.quote_source: Nelson Mandela, Statement from the Dock, Rivonia Trial, Pretoria, 20 April 1964, United Nations archived text
suggested_refs: The capture site on the old Howick road, KwaZulu-Natal
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
Nelson Mandela Capture Site memorial

stops.name: Liliesleaf, the raid that writes the indictment
stops.date_confidence: attested; the geography lens supplies the day, the chronology lens only the month
stops.campa: A dry-cleaning van turns into the Rivonia farm with police inside and takes the entire high command of Umkhonto we Sizwe in a single afternoon: Sisulu, Kathrada, Goldberg, Mbeki, Mhlaba. In the coal shed they find Operation Mayibuye, a plan for guerrilla war, and among the papers the handwriting of a man already serving five years on Robben Island. The state now has its case. Mandela is brought back off the island to stand as Accused Number One in a trial meant to end in a rope.
stops.quote: Sabotage did not involve loss of life, and it offered the best hope for future race relations.
stops.quote_source: Nelson Mandela, Statement from the Dock, Rivonia Trial, Pretoria, 20 April 1964, United Nations archived text
suggested_refs: The Liliesleaf coal shed and the Operation Mayibuye documents
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
Liliesleaf Trust

stops.name: The Old Synagogue, the statement from the dock
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the quotes lens places this statement at -25.7479 / 28.2293, roughly 4 km east of the geography lens's Old Synagogue coordinate. The geography value is used and the conflict is left unresolved
stops.campa: In a synagogue converted into a courtroom, Accused Number One declines to give evidence and instead reads a statement from the dock for four hours and ten minutes. He admits the sabotage and then explains it: that fifty years of non-violence produced only more law, and that sabotage was chosen because it destroys property and not people. The judge does not interrupt him. He puts down his papers for the last paragraph and speaks it looking at the bench, and the room is silent afterwards.
stops.quote: I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities. It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.
stops.quote_source: Nelson Mandela, Statement from the Dock, Rivonia Trial, Pretoria, 20 April 1964, United Nations archived text
suggested_refs: The Old Synagogue courtroom, Pretoria, and the UN's archived text of the statement
sources: Nelson Mandela, Statement from the Dock, Rivonia Trial, Pretoria, 20 April 1964, United Nations archived text
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: The Palace of Justice, the sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested; canonical Pretoria pin inherited byte-identical from muammar_gaddafi.journey.json and jonas_savimbi.journey.json rather than minted anew
stops.campa: Justice Quartus de Wet takes less than three minutes. The crime is in essence high treason, he says, but the state has not charged treason, and so the sentence is life imprisonment rather than death. Eight men are taken down. Outside on the square a crowd sings Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika as the vans pull out. Mandela is forty-five. He will next stand in a public square as a free man when the government sentencing him is out of office and the state it governs has ceased to exist.
stops.quote: During my lifetime I have dedicated myself to this struggle of the African people. I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination.
stops.quote_source: Nelson Mandela, Statement from the Dock, Rivonia Trial, Pretoria, 20 April 1964, United Nations archived text
suggested_refs: The Palace of Justice, Church Square, Pretoria
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'
muammar_gaddafi.journey.json and jonas_savimbi.journey.json (canonical Pretoria pin)

stops.name: Robben Island, cell five in section B
stops.date_confidence: corrected; the chronology lens says he was transferred on the day of sentencing. The flight was overnight and arrived in the early hours of 13 June 1964. The pool carries three near-variant coordinates for the island; the geography value is used
stops.campa: They are flown out overnight and land in the dark. Cell five in the isolation section is seven feet by eight: a straw mat, a sanitary bucket, and a card on the door reading N Mandela 466/64, prisoner four hundred and sixty-six of the year sixty-four. Breakfast is mealie pap. The days are spent breaking rock in the limestone quarry, whose white glare permanently damages his eyes. He is classified group D, permitted one visitor and one letter every six months.
suggested_refs: Cell five, Section B, Robben Island, now the museum's central relic
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
Robben Island Museum

stops.name: The lime quarry, the university
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the quarry years run across the 1960s and 1970s and are not dated to a single year in the record
stops.campa: In the quarry the prisoners talk while they swing hammers, and the talk becomes a curriculum: Sisulu on the history of the Congress, Kathrada on India, Mbeki on economics, Mandela on law, warders leaning on the fence and listening. The prisoners call it the university. Discipline among them is set by their own committee and not by the guards. In 1969 his eldest son Thembekile is killed in a car crash, and the authorities refuse him leave to attend the funeral.
stops.quote: I learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it. The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear.
stops.quote_source: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994); widely quoted but the exact page text could not be independently verified this session, so the attribution is tradition rather than confirmed transcription
suggested_refs: The limestone quarry on Robben Island, worked by the political prisoners for thirteen years
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'
Robben Island Museum

stops.name: Robben Island, the manuscript in the garden
stops.date_confidence: attested; 1975 for the writing and 1976 for the discovery
stops.campa: He writes his life at night, ten pages at a sitting, and passes them to Kathrada and Sisulu, who read, argue, annotate and hand them back. The pages are copied out in microscopic script and the originals buried in cocoa tins in the prison garden he is allowed to keep. In 1976 workmen digging a foundation find them. His study privileges are withdrawn for four years. The copy leaves the island in a departing prisoner's luggage and becomes, eighteen years later, Long Walk to Freedom.
suggested_refs: The buried manuscript of Long Walk to Freedom, Robben Island prison garden
sources: South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Pollsmoor, the rooftop and the first talks
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the geography lens coordinate -34.048 / 18.413 is roughly 4 km off, into Tokai and Constantia, and is corrected here to the prison's location on Steenberg Road. The corrected value is approximate
stops.campa: Without explanation he and three colleagues are taken off the island and put in a large cell on the top floor of a mainland prison, with beds, a radio and a strip of roof where he grows onions and aubergines in oil drums. The isolation is the point: the government is separating him from the collective that decides things. Winnie is allowed to touch him for the first time in twenty-one years. Within three years the men who moved him are sending emissaries up the stairs to ask what terms he might consider.
suggested_refs: Pollsmoor Maximum Security Prison, Steenberg Road, Tokai, Cape Town
sources: Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)
South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'

stops.name: Jabulani Stadium, the offer refused
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the chronology lens merges this event with P.W. Botha's offer of 31 January 1985 and places it in 'South Africa'. The stadium coordinate is not carried by the verified pool and is approximate
stops.campa: P.W. Botha stands in Parliament and offers him release if he will renounce violence as a political instrument. Ten days later, in a stadium in Soweto, his daughter Zindzi reads his answer aloud to the crowd, the first words of his heard in public in twenty-one years. He asks what freedom is being offered to a man whose organisation is banned, and reminds them which side turned to violence first. The crowd carries the last line out of the stadium and into the townships.
suggested_refs: Jabulani Stadium, Soweto, and the UDF rally of 10 February 1985
sources: South African History Online, 'Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela'
Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (Little, Brown, 1994)

stops.name: Victor Verster, the warder's cottage
stops.date_confidence: corrected; the chronology lens gives 7 December 1988, which is the date of his transfer to the Constantiaberg Medi-Clinic, and dates the tuberculosis to August 1985, which was in fact prostate surgery. The geography lens coordinate -33.811 / 19.021 is replaced by the afterlife lens value
stops.campa: Tuberculosis is diagnosed after fluid is drained from his lung, and after two months in hospital he is moved not to a cell but to a warder's house inside a prison farm near Paarl: three bedrooms, a swimming pool, a cook seconded from the prison service. Ministers come to lunch. He receives them alone, without the Congress's authority to negotiate, and says so at every meeting. For fourteen months the state keeps one prisoner in a house and negotiates with him about its own ending.
suggested_refs: The warder's cottage at Victor Verster Prison, now a national heritage site

stops.name: Victor Verster, the walk out of the gate
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nine days after F.W. de Klerk unbans the Congress in Parliament, Mandela walks the last three hundred metres to the prison gate on foot, holding Winnie's hand, and raises a clenched fist into a wall of cameras. He is seventy-one. He has been in prison for twenty-seven years and six months, and no photograph of him has been lawfully published in South Africa in any of them. The country watching on television expects a young boxer and is shown an old man in a grey suit.

stops.name: Cape Town City Hall, the balcony over the Grand Parade
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is driven into a city that has kept him offshore for eighteen years and speaks from the City Hall balcony over the Grand Parade, so late that the light is going and he has to borrow reading glasses. He greets the crowd in the name of peace, democracy and freedom for all, then says the part they came for: that the armed struggle is not over, and that he stands before them not as a prophet but as a servant. Robben Island is visible from the square, and so is the parliament where Cecil Rhodes, as Cape premier, twice narrowed the franchise this crowd is still waiting to be given.

stops.name: Wembley Stadium, the seventy thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Two months out of prison he walks onto a stage at Wembley in front of seventy thousand people and a television audience across sixty countries, at a concert staged by the movement that spent thirty years asking governments to boycott his jailers. He thanks them by their trades: the dockers who would not unload, the students who emptied the shelves, the musicians who would not play Sun City. The applause runs for several minutes before he is able to begin speaking.

stops.name: United Nations, the committee against apartheid
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He addresses the committee the General Assembly created to isolate his country, and asks it not to stop. Sanctions must stay, he says, until the process is irreversible, because a government that has so far conceded nothing but a conversation may concede nothing further. New York gives him a ticker-tape parade up Broadway. He is a private citizen of a state that still denies him a vote, received in every capital he enters with the honours due a head of state.

stops.name: Oslo City Hall, the prize shared with the last president
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He takes the Nobel Peace Prize standing beside F.W. de Klerk, the last president of apartheid, eight months after the assassination of Chris Hani at Boksburg brought the country nearer open war than any day of the negotiations. It was Mandela, holding no office at all, who went on state television that night and asked South Africans not to answer the killing in kind. In Oslo he credits the dead who will not vote, and the ordinary people whose sacrifice paid for the ceremony.

stops.name: Ohlange Institute, the vote beside Dube's grave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the chronology lens places this vote in Durban, corrected here to the Ohlange Institute at Inanda, some 25 km north. The geography lens coordinate -29.6675 / 30.927 is about 4.5 km off and is corrected
stops.campa: He could have voted anywhere in the country. He drives instead to a school in the hills north of Durban founded in 1901 by John Langalibalele Dube, the first president of the African National Congress, lays a wreath on Dube's grave in the grounds, and then goes inside and marks a ballot for the first time at the age of seventy-five. Mr Dube, he says afterwards, I have come to report that South Africa is now free. The queues that day run for hours and nobody leaves them.

stops.name: The Union Buildings, the inauguration
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is sworn in on the terraces of the building from which the state that imprisoned him was administered, with de Klerk and Thabo Mbeki as his deputies and the commanders of the security forces standing behind him. Jets of the air force that bombed Congress houses in three neighbouring countries trail the colours of the new flag overhead and dip their wings. The generals who would have hanged him salute. He serves a single term and does not stand for a second.
stops.quote: No one is born hating another person because of the color of his skin, or his background, or his religion. People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love, for love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite.

stops.name: Pretoria, the friend in Tripoli
stops.date_confidence: attested; canonical Pretoria pin inherited byte-identical from muammar_gaddafi.journey.json, which carries a dedicated stop naming Mandela
stops.campa: President Mandela flies to Tripoli against a Western air embargo and Washington's open objection, and is told by American officials that Muammar Gaddafi is not a man a democracy receives. His answer is that those who backed the struggle when backing it was illegal are not discarded once it becomes respectable. Libya funded the Congress. So did Fidel Castro, whose troops fought the South African army in Angola, the same army that armed Jonas Savimbi and kept Mandela on an island.

stops.name: Houghton, the house in the forbidden suburb
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1999 for the retirement; the day is inferred
stops.campa: He hands the presidency to Thabo Mbeki after one term, an African head of state leaving office alive, willingly and on schedule, and retires to a walled house in a Johannesburg suburb where until recently the law forbade him to sleep. From there he runs a foundation, raises money for schools and clinics, founds the Elders, and in 2005 stands in front of the cameras to say that his son Makgatho has died of AIDS, in a country where the disease is still named in euphemisms.

stops.name: Howick, the memorial of fifty columns
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Wikipedia pages for the capture site and its memorial returned HTTP 404 this session, so the sculptor and the unveiling date are recorded as consistently attested rather than verified against a live source
stops.campa: Fifty years to the day after the roadblock, fifty steel columns are raised in a field beside the Durban road, each a black bar planted at its own depth and angle, so that walking past shows only a thicket of iron. At thirty-five metres, from one point on the path, the columns close and become his face. The sculptor is Marco Cianfanelli. It is unveiled on the anniversary itself, thirteen years after he left office. From anywhere else on the path the face is not there.

stops.name: Houghton, the death of an old man
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies at home at ninety-five after a long respiratory illness, the lungs damaged by tuberculosis and by seventeen years of limestone dust. The president announces it to the country after midnight. Crowds gather in the street outside the house through the night with candles, and the noise from Vilakazi Street in Soweto, where the two-room house still stands, is dancing rather than mourning, which is what he had asked for. Ninety-one governments begin arranging flights.

The lying in state at the Union Buildings runs for three days afterwards, in the same building where he was sworn in nineteen years before, and the queues along the lawns do not shorten.

stops.name: Qunu, the grave in the hills
stops.date_confidence: attested; the afterlife lens gives -31.9333 / 28.7833 for the burial, roughly 22 km east into open country, corrected here to the geography lens's Qunu coordinate, which the same pool carries twice
stops.campa: He is buried on the family ground at Qunu after a state funeral, in the valley where he herded calves and moulded clay oxen ninety-five years before. Some four and a half thousand people attend; the graveside rites are Thembu and closed to cameras. Five months earlier a court ordered the remains of three of his children returned to this ground from Mvezo, where a grandson had moved them. The mission school that gave him the name Nelson stands a short walk off.
